newsitem.title: USA: CBOT's new inflation-indexed notes to face hurdles.
newsitem.headline: CBOT's new inflation-indexed notes to face hurdles.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade's introduction of futures and options on inflation-protected U.S. Treasury notes Thursday will take place in a difficult market environment, traders and analysts said.
The CBOT will begin trade in derivatives on five- and 10-year inflation-indexed Treasury securities on Thursday. Similar products based on an inflation-protected 30-year issue are planned for 1998.
Chief among the obstacles the infant contracts will face is low U.S. inflation, market participants said. Another early challenge for the derivatives is low liquidity in the cash market.
"I don't think the expectations are very high for initial trading," said a floor broker in Treasury futures.

Sylvie Bouriaux, CBOT's group manager for financial research and product development, predicted a moderate start to trading but said the exchange markets would deepen as the supply of inflation-indexed debt grows.
"At the beginning we do expect dealers to come and hedge their exposure, and down the road institutional users as well," she said.

When the exchange's benchmark 30-year bond futures contract made its debut in the late 1970s, she noted, total outstanding issuance in the underlying security was a tiny sliver of what it would later become.
To date, the Treasury has held just two auctions of inflation-indexed securities. It sold $7 billion of the 10-year notes in January and reopened the issue in April, auctioning another $8 billion.
The first sale was oversubscribed, but the second drew tepid interest, making it even more difficult to gauge the securities' full potential, analysts said.
"Nobody really knows how deep the market is in terms of demand. There is still a lot of discovery that needs to be done," said Steven Wood, managing director for BancAmerica Securities Inc.
At 1430 EDT/1830 GMT, the Treasury will announce the size of the inaugural auction of five-year inflation-indexed notes, to be held July 8. The securities will settle July 15.
Investors in inflation-indexed securities are shielded from inflation because the principal value of the debt is adjusted regularly for changes in the Consumer Price Index.
"It's hard to get excited about a security that protects you against rising inflation when inflation isn't rising," Wood said.
However, those who purchase inflation-indexed securities still face interest rate risk, and the CBOT products provide a vehicle for hedging against such volatility in real yields, Bouriaux said.

The new contracts will trade alongside the regular five- and 10-year futures and options in their respective pits. Trading hours are 0720-1400 CDT, same as for the conventional contracts. The new products initially will not be listed on the Project A after-hours system.
